cards.title: 1.1 Rate of a Chemical Reaction and Collision Theory
body: 1.1 Rate of a Chemical Reaction and Collision Theory

**Rate of reaction** is defined as the measure of how fast the reactants are converted into products, represented quantitatively as the change in the concentration of a reactant or a product per unit of time: $$ \\text{Rate} = -\\frac{\\Delta[\\text{Reactant}]}{\\Delta t} = \\frac{\\Delta[\\text{Product}]}{\\Delta t} $$.

In chemical kinetics, understanding the speed of a process is just as crucial as knowing the final products. Some chemical reactions occur almost instantaneously, such as the precipitation of silver chloride when silver nitrate and sodium chloride solutions are mixed, or the explosive combustion of hydrogen gas. In contrast, other reactions occur over incredibly long time spans. The rusting of iron doors in classrooms or the slow weathering of silicate rocks on mountain surfaces are prime examples of processes

cards.title: Rate of a Chemical Reaction and Factors Affecting It
body: However, rate is not a static property; it changes continuously as a reaction proceeds because the concentration of the reactants decreases. The average rate provides a general overview of the reaction's speed over a specific time interval, but it does not tell the full story. For a more precise understanding, chemists plot concentration against time and determine the instantaneous rate, which is the slope of the tangent to the curve at a specific point in time.

body: Second, the colliding particles must possess a minimum amount of kinetic energy, known as the activation energy ($$E_a$$). Activation energy represents the energy barrier that reactants must climb to break their existing chemical bonds and form an unstable transition state called the activated complex. If particles collide with less energy than $$E_a$$, they simply bounce off one another elastically and remain chemically unchanged.

| **Temperature** | Increases average kinetic energy and the fraction of particles exceeding $$E_a$$ | Food spoils faster at room temperature than in a refrigerator |

### 📝 Topic Challenge (Moderate to Hard)
1. Explain why a $$10^\\circ\\text{C}$$ rise in temperature can double a reaction rate even though it only increases the average kinetic energy of the molecules by a very small percentage.
*Answer:* A $$10^\\circ\\text{C}$$ increase raises the average kinetic energy slightly, but it drastically increases the *fraction of molecules* that possess kinetic energy equal to or greater than the activation energy ($$E \\ge E_a$$), as shown by the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curve.

cards.title: 1.2 Reversible Reactions and Chemical Equilibrium
body: 1.2 Reversible Reactions and Chemical Equilibrium

**Chemical Equilibrium** is defined as a state in a reversible reaction where the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction, leading to constant concentrations of reactants and products over time: $$ \\text{Rate}_{\\text{forward}} = \\text{Rate}_{\\text{reverse}} $$.

In general, chemical reactions can be categorized as irreversible or reversible. Irreversible reactions proceed in only one direction, continuing until at least one of the reactants is completely consumed. Examples include the burning of hydrocarbons or the reaction of active metals with strong acids. On the other hand, in a reversible reaction, the products can react to reform the original reactants under suitable conditions. This bidirectional nature is symbolized by a double arrow ($$\\rightleftharpoons$$).

cards.title: Study Notes worked
cards.problem: A chemical system reaches dynamic equilibrium when:

steps.text: Chemical equilibrium is a dynamic state. This means the reactions do not stop, but rather occur in both directions simultaneously.
At equilibrium, the forward rate of reaction equals the reverse rate of reaction.
Because the rates are equal, the net concentrations of reactants and products remain constant, but they are not necessarily equal in value.

cards.title: Study Notes worked
cards.problem: If the forward reaction of a system in equilibrium is endothermic, increasing the temperature of the system will:

steps.text: **Step 1: Treat heat as a reactant or product**
For an endothermic reaction, heat is absorbed: $$\\text{Reactants} + \\text{Heat} \\rightleftharpoons \\text{Products}$$.
Increasing temperature is equivalent to adding heat to the reactant side.
To consume the added heat, the system shifts to the **right** (towards products).

cards.title: Study Notes worked
cards.problem: According to the Collision Theory, reactant particles must collide with:

steps.text: **Step 1: Identify key criteria of Collision Theory**
Collision Theory requires three things for a reaction to occur: collisions, sufficient energy, and correct orientation.
The colliding particles must have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy ($$E_a$$).
They must align correctly so that reactive bonds can break and new ones can form.

To study these kinetics systematically, chemists must measure the rate of a reaction. This is done by tracking a physical or chemical parameter over time. Commonly monitored properties include the volume of a gas evolved using a gas syringe system, the loss or gain of mass of a reaction vessel on a digital balance, changes in the color intensity of a solution using a colorimeter, shifts in pH level for acid-base reactions, changes in temperature, or fluctuations in electrical conductivity as ions are produced or consumed.

cards.title: Rate of a Chemical Reaction and Factors Affecting It
body: To explain how these reaction rates are controlled at the molecular level, chemists rely on the Collision Theory. According to this theory, three essential criteria must be met for a chemical reaction to occur. First, the reacting molecules, atoms, or ions must physically collide with one another. A higher number of collisions per unit time establishes a greater probability of chemical transformation, which directly explains why increasing reactant concentration or temperature typically accelerates reaction rates.

cards.title: Rate of a Chemical Reaction and Factors Affecting It
body: Third, the collision must occur with the proper spatial orientation. For complex or asymmetrical molecules, the reactive sites must align perfectly during the collision. For example, in the addition reaction between ethene ($$CH_2=CH_2$$) and hydrogen chloride ($$HCl$$) to form chloroethane ($$CH_3CH_2Cl$$), the hydrogen end of the $$HCl$$ molecule must specifically approach the carbon-carbon double bond. Any other collision geometry, such as the chlorine end striking a carbon atom first, fails to initiate bond rearrangement, causing the molecules to rebound without reacting.

Without these enzymes, vital metabolic reactions—such as the digestion of sugars—would take weeks to occur at normal body temperature ($$37^\\circ\\text{C}$$), rendering life impossible!

cards.title: Study Notes worked
cards.problem: For the equilibrium system: $$2S(s) + 5F_2(g) \\rightleftharpoons SF_4(g) + SF_6(g)$$, in which direction will the equilibrium shift if the pressure of the system is increased?

steps.text: **Step 1: Apply Le Chatelier's Principle for pressure**
Increasing pressure shifts the equilibrium to the side with fewer moles of gas.
**Step 2: Count gas moles on reactant side**
Only gases are counted. $$2S(s)$$ is solid. Gaseous reactant is $$5F_2(g)$$, which is **$$5\\text{ moles}$$**.
**Step 3: Count gas moles on product side**
Gaseous products are $$SF_4(g)$$ and $$SF_6(g)$$, which represent $$1 + 1 = \\mathbf{2\\text{ moles}}$$.

cards.title: Study Notes worked
cards.problem: What is the primary action of a catalyst in a chemical reaction?

steps.text: A catalyst is a substance that increases the rate of reaction without being consumed.
It does not change temperature or kinetic energy. It does not alter thermodynamic properties like $$K_c$$.
It lowers the activation energy ($$E_a$$) by providing an alternative mechanism (pathway). This allows more molecules to successfully react per unit time.

cards.title: Study Notes worked
cards.problem: If the reaction quotient $$Q_c$$ is less than the equilibrium constant $$K_c$$ ($$Q_c < K_c$$), the system will:

steps.text: $$Q_c$$ measures the ratio of products to reactants at any given moment. $$K_c$$ is this ratio at equilibrium.
Since the ratio is smaller than required, there are not enough products or too many reactants.
To increase products and reach equilibrium, the reaction must proceed in the forward direction (shifts to the **right**).
